draft.title: The unemployment rate
card: The labour force is everyone aged 15 or over who has a job or is actively looking for one. People who are not working and not looking, such as full-time students and retirees, are outside it.
A person is unemployed if they have no job, are looking for work and are available to start. Someone who works even a few hours a week is counted as employed.
Unemployment rate = unemployed people ÷ labour force × 100. For example, 50 unemployed people in a labour force of 1000 gives a rate of 5%.
High unemployment wastes resources, because people who could work are idle. It also lowers living standards, because households have less income to spend.
draft.remember: Unemployment rate = unemployed people as a share of the labour force, not of the whole population. High unemployment wastes resources.

a.q: Who would be counted as unemployed in the official figures?
opts: Leila, who has no job and is applying for work
Sam, who is retired and does not want a job
Priya, who is studying full time and not job hunting
Tom, who works six hours a week at a bakery
a.why: Leila has no job, is looking for work and is available, so she is unemployed. Tom is employed because he works some hours, even though it is not many.
a.clue: Unemployed people want work and are looking for it.

b.q: A town in Victoria, such as Shepparton, has a labour force of 2000 people. Of these, 100 are unemployed. What is its unemployment rate?
b.why: The rate is unemployed people divided by the labour force: 100 ÷ 2000 × 100 = 5%. The tempting answer is 95%, which is the share of the labour force with a job.
b.clue: Divide by the labour force, then multiply by 100.

a.best: Leila, who has no job and is applying for work

problems.detail: "A town in Victoria, such as Shepparton, has a labour force of 2000 people" reads as if Shepparton's labour force is 2000. Shepparton is a regional city of tens of thousands of people, so students could take away a wrong fact. Use an unnamed or clearly hypothetical town.

check.summary: The definitions and the calculation are correct, and both questions have one clear answer. Question b's wording suggests Shepparton has a labour force of only 2000, which is far too small; use a hypothetical town instead.
